title: AMD Advancing AI 2026 Keynote Live Coverage
gist: Live coverage of AMD's Advancing AI 2026 keynote, where Lisa Su launched Helios — AMD's first rack-scale system (MI455X with 432GB HBM4, EPYC Venice on TSMC 2nm up to 256 cores, Pensando NICs) — in full production with Q3 shipments and an H2 2027 ramp, alongside a 2GW Anthropic commitment and OpenAI's in-progress 6GW deployment. AMD sized the 2030 AI accelerator TAM at $1.4T (CPUs $220B, total silicon $2T at 40% CAGR), claimed 46% server CPU revenue share, 2.2x per-socket performance versus NVIDIA Vera, 30% more tokens per dollar than the competition, and pushed ROCm.AI built on Codex and Claude with a 3.3x inference gain over ROCm 7.

insights.claim: AMD now expects the AI accelerator total addressable market to reach $1.4T in 2030 — the size of the entire chip market today.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: The anchor number behind AMD's data-center investment case; any accelerator-market model materially below this implies AMD is over-earning on expectations.
insights.quote: AMD now expects the TAM for the AI accelerator market to reach $1.4T in 2030. It will be the size of the entire chip market today.

insights.claim: AMD projects the CPU market alone will be worth $220B in 2030, arguing agentic AI needs large amounts of CPU to run agent tasks and orchestrate GPUs, not just GPUs.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Reframes CPUs as an AI-levered growth market rather than a mature one — the core of AMD's argument that EPYC benefits from the same wave as Instinct.
insights.quote: The CPU market will be a $220B market in 2030.

insights.claim: AMD expects a 40% CAGR toward a $2T total addressable market for silicon by 2030.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: A 40% compound growth assumption for total silicon is aggressive versus historical semiconductor cycles — the key assumption to stress-test.
insights.quote: Altogether, AMD is expecting a 40% CAGR for a total addressable market for silicon of $2T by 2030.

insights.claim: Inference has now overtaken training: more AI compute capacity is used for inference than for training, and the shift to agentic AI is growing the accelerator market significantly because agents need far more compute than earlier AI chatbots.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: An inference-dominated mix favors memory capacity, tokens-per-dollar and CPU orchestration over raw training FLOPS — the competitive terrain AMD is choosing.
insights.quote: Inference has now overtaken compute. More AI compute capacity is used for inference than training.

insights.claim: Model performance is improving faster than hardware performance is improving, and the rate and pace of agentic AI adoption has run ahead of AMD's own expectations.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: If software gains outrun hardware gains, compute demand per unit of capability falls — a subtle bear signal buried inside a bullish keynote.
insights.quote: The performance improvement of models is faster than the rate of performance improvements from hardware.

insights.claim: AMD launched Helios, its first rack-scale AI system, fusing MI455X GPUs, EPYC Venice CPUs and Pensando Vulcano DPUs/NICs into a single rack with a scale-up network so the rack functions as one machine — AMD's answer to NVIDIA's NVL72.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: AMD now competes at the rack level rather than the chip level, which is where hyperscaler purchasing decisions are actually made.
insights.quote: Helios is the fusion of AMD’s MI455X GPUs, EPYC “Venice” CPUs, and Pensando DPUs, with a complete system fitting into a single rack and employing a speedy scale-up networking architecture to allow the rack to function as a single machine.

insights.claim: Helios is in full production with shipments starting in Q3 and ramping into the second half of 2027.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: A concrete revenue-timing marker: meaningful Helios revenue lands in late 2026 with the volume ramp in H2 2027, not immediately.
insights.quote: Announcing today that Helios is in full production. Shipments will start in Q3. Ramping into the second half of 2027.

insights.claim: The MI455X uses 2nm compute chiplets with 3nm elsewhere, multiple compute dies and 432GB of HBM4 memory, mounted on an Enhanced Accelerator Module (EAM).
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: 432GB of HBM4 per accelerator is the specific memory-capacity claim AMD is using to win inference workloads — and a large HBM4 demand line for memory suppliers.
insights.quote: Recapping the MI455X architecture. 2nm compute chiplets, 3nm elsewhere. Multiple compute dies, 432GB of HBM4 memory.

insights.claim: AMD claims Helios delivers 50% more memory capacity and 15% more FP4 performance, is 10-15% more performant in a power-limited context, and yields 30% more tokens per dollar than the competition.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Tokens-per-dollar and power efficiency, not peak FLOPS, are the metrics AMD is competing on — the frame to use when comparing against NVIDIA racks.
insights.quote: AMD says Helios is 10-15% more performant here. Leading to 30% more tokens per dollar than the competition.

insights.claim: AMD claims MI455X delivers up to 34x faster token throughput than the prior-generation MI355X.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: A generational claim large enough to require scrutiny of the workload and precision assumptions behind it before modeling ASP or share gains.
insights.quote: MI455X vs. MI355X: Up to 34x faster token throughput.

insights.claim: Power is the binding limiter on AI deployments right now, so efficiency is what allows a given investment to serve more users.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: If power, not silicon supply, is the constraint, perf-per-watt leadership converts directly into share — and grid capacity becomes the sector's real bottleneck.
insights.quote: Power is the big limiter right now, so efficiency is a need.

insights.claim: Anthropic will buy 2GW of Helios hardware from AMD for its own use, with Lisa Su framing it as the start of a multi-year partnership focused on scale-up and on security from the chip level up to whole racks.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: A named 2GW commitment from a frontier lab is the strongest validation yet that AMD is a genuine second source for training-class compute.
insights.quote: This week AMD and Anthropic announced that Anthropic will be buying 2GW of Helios hardware from AMD for their own use.

insights.claim: OpenAI is still deploying the 6GW of AMD hardware it announced last year, received a pre-production Helios rack a few months ago, expects to start deploying Helios by the end of this year and accelerate into 2027, and is already looking ahead to MI500 in 2027.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Confirms the 6GW OpenAI commitment is mid-deployment rather than aspirational, and puts Helios deployment inside calendar 2026.
insights.quote: OpenAI is still in the process of deploying their 6GW of AMD hardware that they announced last year.

insights.claim: Meta says it now thinks about whole data centers as a single system rather than about CPUs, considers CPUs to be becoming as important as GPUs if not more so, co-developed the rack-scale OCP standards with AMD, and wants to sit down today to co-design what will be deployed in 2028.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Hyperscaler co-design cycles now run roughly two years ahead, meaning 2028 competitive position is being locked in now — a moat for incumbent suppliers.
insights.quote: The earlier we co-design, the better we are.

insights.claim: AT&T is burning about a trillion tokens per month, uses AI for planning equipment deployment as well as customer relations and transcription, and credits AMD's open-systems focus with letting it drive down token costs and hold total token spending flat despite rising consumption.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: A rare hard enterprise inference volume number plus evidence that unit token costs are falling fast enough to offset volume growth — bearish for pure inference-revenue growth models.
insights.quote: AT&T is burning about a trillion tokens per month.

insights.claim: Cerebras is partnering with AMD on a disaggregated solution in which Helios does the heavy lifting behind its wafer-scale engine for ultra-low-latency inference, delivering 5x the performance of the wafer-scale engine alone and shipping in Cerebras's cloud service later this year.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Heterogeneous multi-accelerator inference stacks are becoming real products, mirroring NVIDIA's Groq pairing — a new architecture category to track.
insights.quote: The combination of Helios plus the wafer scale engine will allow Cerebras to deliver ULL with Helios providing heavy lifting in the background. 5x the performance of the wafer scale engine alone.

insights.claim: AMD says it is now at 46% revenue share in the server CPU market.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Approaching revenue parity with Intel in server CPUs — the single most important structural datapoint for both companies' data-center P&Ls.
insights.quote: AMD is now up to 46% of revenue share in the server CPU market.

insights.claim: EPYC Venice is built on Zen 6 on TSMC 2nm with up to 256 cores per socket and delivers higher IPC and higher frequency than Turin/Zen 5 in what AMD calls one of the largest generational gains in EPYC history.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: 2nm at 256 cores resets the server core-count and performance bar, pressuring both Intel and Arm-based server entrants on the same node timeline.
insights.quote: Zen 6 delivers higher IPC and higher frequency than Turin/Zen 5.

insights.claim: Venice ships as a family: Venice HF (the high-frequency part inside Helios), a dense 256-core version, a 128-core general compute version, and Venice-X with 3D stacked cache in which the cache chiplets sit below the compute chiplets.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Cache-below-compute is an inversion of AMD's prior 3D V-Cache stacking order, with thermal implications that favor higher clocks — a real engineering differentiator.
insights.quote: As well as Venice-X, which will feature 3D stacked cache with the cache chiplets below the compute chiplets.

insights.claim: AMD claims Venice delivers 2x the performance per watt for agents versus the competition, an even wider gap versus Arm competitors, and 2.2x performance per socket versus NVIDIA's Vera, explicitly emphasizing total chip throughput and x86 software compatibility.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: AMD is countering Arm server CPUs on throughput per socket rather than per core — the exact framing dispute that determines Vera's competitive impact.
insights.quote: And versus NVIDIA’s Vera? 2.2x performance per socket. i.e. AMD focusing on total chip throughput.

insights.claim: Venice is in full production with customer demand described as higher than ever before, and AMD offers EPYC SKUs spanning 8 to 256 cores across multiple chip designs because no single SKU covers all enterprise needs.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Breadth of SKU coverage is AMD's defense of enterprise share against both Intel and specialized Arm parts targeting narrow segments.
insights.quote: Venice is in full production. Customer demand is higher than ever before.

insights.claim: AMD's forward roadmap commits to Florence with Zen 7 in 2028 and Rivenna with Zen 8 under development for 2030, plus a new Instinct generation every year (MI600 with CDNA Next in 2028) and a new rack-scale system every year.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: An annual cadence commitment across CPU, GPU and rack matches NVIDIA's tempo — the operational promise investors should hold AMD to.
insights.quote: 2028 will bring Florence with Zen 7. Supports latest memory technologies. And Rivenna Zen 8 is under development for 2030.

insights.claim: AMD claims MI500 will deliver the largest generational leap in its Instinct history, characterized as a 2000x performance improvement in just four years.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: An extraordinary cumulative claim that only holds under specific precision and workload definitions — verify the baseline before using it in any model.
insights.quote: Meanwhile MI500 will deliver the largest generational leap in performance. 2000x performance improvement in just 4 years.

insights.claim: MI430X targets the HPC market with hardware FP64 at 288 TFLOPS and the same memory capabilities as MI455X, shipping in H1 2027 and built by swapping MI455X compute dies for FP64 compute dies within AMD's chiplet strategy.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Demonstrates the economic payoff of chiplets — a distinct HPC SKU created by die substitution rather than a new design, protecting AMD's supercomputer franchise.
insights.quote: MI430X will target the HPC market with strong FP64 performance. Intended to deliver leadership performance for HPC with hardware FP64. 288 TFLOPS FP64.

insights.claim: ROCm is now shipping releases every six weeks instead of every few months, and the latest release improves inference performance by 3.3x over ROCm 7 and training performance by 2.4x.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Software-only performance gains of this size mean installed AMD hardware is appreciating in value — the historical weak point of the AMD case is closing.
insights.quote: The latest ROCm release improves inference performance by 3.3x over ROCm 7. And training performance by 2.4x.

insights.claim: AMD introduced ROCm.AI, underpinned by major coding AI agents such as Codex and Claude with AMD's own tools layered on top, including AMD-created skills for ROCm and Hyperloom, a code and performance optimization tool.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: AMD is outsourcing developer-experience parity with CUDA to third-party coding agents — a cheaper path to closing the software moat than hiring kernel engineers.
insights.quote: Underpinned by major coding AI agents such as Codex and Claude. But with AMD’s tools on top.

insights.claim: In a live demo, AMD's Hyperloom tool improved the token rate of the code it optimized by 38%.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: A concrete measure of automated kernel optimization value — the mechanism by which AMD closes the CUDA performance gap without developer effort.
insights.quote: Hyperloom was able to improve the token rate of the code by 38%.

insights.claim: AMD's own engineers are already using AI tools to write AI GPU kernels, and OpenAI's Triton creator says models have reached the point of generating high-quality kernels, something they were not good at before, crediting AMD's embrace of open source.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: If AI can generate competitive kernels, CUDA's hand-tuned library advantage erodes — the single biggest structural threat to NVIDIA's software moat.
insights.quote: Models are getting to the point where they’re capable of generating high-quality kernels, something they weren’t good at before.

insights.claim: Day-zero model readiness is described as a huge deal for AMD and is something ROCm.AI enables.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Day-0 support for new models is the practical purchase criterion for inference buyers — a metric to track release-by-release against NVIDIA.
insights.quote: Meanwhile day-0 readiness is a huge deal for AMD. And it’s something that ROCm.AI enables.

themes.theme: Enterprise, client and physical AI expansion

insights.claim: AMD launched the Instinct MI350P, a PCIe-form-factor version of its MI350 accelerator, and is comparing it against NVIDIA's Hopper-generation PCIe cards because NVIDIA has no Blackwell-generation PCIe card.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: A genuine product gap in NVIDIA's lineup — PCIe-slot enterprise AI is an addressable segment where AMD faces an older competing part.
insights.quote: Making performance comparisons to NVIDIA’s Hopper-generation PCIe cards (they don’t have a Blackwell generation PCIe card).

insights.claim: AMD's earliest internal AI deployments targeted autonomous threat detection and a personalized AI assistant running on OpenClaw, where intelligent routing reduced token costs by 43%.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Model routing cutting token costs 43% is a direct signal that inference spend per task is deflating faster than usage models assume.
insights.quote: Intelligent routing reduced token costs by 43%.

insights.claim: On the client side, AMD says QWEN 3.5 outperformed GPT-OSS within seven months using a fraction of the parameters, Ryzen AI already supports up to 9B-parameter models, and Gorgon Halo will be Strix Halo with 192GB of LPDDR5X — 64GB more than Strix.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Small-model efficiency gains plus 192GB of local memory make on-device inference viable, shifting some inference demand away from data-center capacity.
insights.quote: In 7 months, QWEN 3.5 has outperformed GPT-OSS with a fraction of the parameters.

insights.claim: Starting later this year every AMD Halo developer box will include a year's subscription to Hugging Face Pro, part of AMD's argument that personal AI is now a category rather than a concept.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Bundling a developer-ecosystem subscription is a cheap distribution play for building an AMD-native local-AI developer base.
insights.quote: Personal AI is not a concept. It is a category.

insights.claim: AMD is entering physical AI with the Kria AI System on Module powered by the Ryzen AI Embedded X100 plus a Kria AI dev kit containing a Kria SOM and an Ultrascale+ FPGA, explicitly targeting NVIDIA's Jetson Thor and Jetson dev kits.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: AMD is monetizing the Xilinx acquisition against a NVIDIA franchise with no credible second source — robotics silicon is the next contested segment.
insights.quote: AMD is gunning for NVIDIA’s Jetson Thor.

insights.claim: Cisco argues inference will be distributed everywhere rather than confined to servers, requiring security, network bandwidth and tools to contain token cost and usage, with general availability of its management tools expected this fall.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Token-cost governance is emerging as a distinct enterprise software category — an adjacency for networking and observability vendors.
insights.quote: AI is moving closer to employees; compute will need to move closer as well.

insights.claim: AMD's Advancing AI has grown from a press conference into a full trade show filling all of Moscone Center West, effectively becoming AMD's equivalent of NVIDIA's GTC just 60 miles down the road.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Event scale is a soft but real indicator of ecosystem gravity — AMD is now able to convene the AI supply chain in the way only NVIDIA previously could.
insights.quote: The event has effectively turned into AMD’s equivalent to NVIDIA’s GTC – just 60 miles down the road.
